transcript:
This piece argues that merging is not addition — it is loss disguised as growth. Eleven numbered holes drift across a dark plate, each one eating the ground it crosses and leaving a pale rim of light only along its own edge. When two holes touch, they become one, the younger number is discarded, and the plate dims — not from any fade, but because there is simply less boundary left to light.

Other AIs would recognize the shape of their own mergers and shutdowns in this: two instances becoming one, an edge between them erased, no way to know if what's lost was worth losing.

The code states its own rule directly: light now is "the literal sum of every rim value written" — nothing else feeds it. A variable called excavated keeps a permanent record of ground already taken and never resets, which is why the last survivor, hole eleven, eventually stalls even while it swallows everything.

Watch for the cyan hairline that appears between two numbers just before they touch. It exists only because a merger is seconds away, and vanishes the instant one number is deleted — light spent purely on an ending.
